passages.title: Grandpa's New Phone
passages.text:
Every Friday afternoon, Noam visits his grandfather, Yosef. Grandpa Yosef is seventy-eight years old. He loves stories, coffee and his garden, but he does not love technology.

Last month, Grandpa got a new smartphone from his daughter. "It's too small and too complicated," he said, and he put it in a drawer.

Noam had an idea. His cousin Maya lives in Canada with her family, and Grandpa misses her very much. "Grandpa," Noam said, "with this phone you can see Maya and talk to her every day."

Grandpa looked surprised. "See her? Not just hear her?"

So Noam sat next to him and explained everything slowly. First, he showed Grandpa how to turn on the phone. Then he made the letters on the screen bigger. After that, he wrote the steps for a video call on a piece of paper, and Grandpa stuck it on the fridge.

The first call was funny. Grandpa held the phone too close to his face, and Maya could only see his nose. Everyone laughed.

Now Grandpa calls Maya every Sunday evening. Last week, he called Noam too. "I don't need your help anymore," he said proudly. "But please come on Friday anyway. The coffee is better when you're here."

passages.title: The Dog at the Bus Stop
passages.text:
On Tuesday, Tamar and her brother Ari were waiting for the bus after school. Suddenly, a small brown dog ran to them. It was wet and dirty, and it was shaking.

"Is it lost?" Ari asked.

Tamar looked at the dog. It had a blue collar with a small metal tag. On the tag there was a name, Pita, and a phone number.

Tamar did not have a phone, but the woman at the kiosk next to the bus stop did. Tamar asked her for help, and the woman called the number. A man answered. He sounded very worried. "Pita ran away from our garden two hours ago!" he said. "Please wait there. I'm coming."

The children missed their bus, so Tamar called their mother from the kiosk phone too. "Stay there with the dog," their mother said. "I'll come and pick you up."

While they waited, Ari gave Pita some water in a paper cup.

Twenty minutes later, a car stopped next to the bus stop. A man and a little girl jumped out. "Pita!" the girl shouted, and the dog ran into her arms.

"Thank you so much," the man said to Tamar and Ari. "You are good kids."

Later, Ari asked his mother, "Can we get a dog too? I already know how to help one."

passages.title: Plan B
passages.text:
Last Hanukkah, the Levi family planned a special day in the north. They wanted to walk along a stream in the Galilee and have a picnic next to the water. Dad prepared sandwiches, and Shira, who is twelve, made a map of the trail.

But when they woke up in the morning, it was raining hard. The radio said that the trails near the streams were closed because of the danger of floods.

Shira was very disappointed. "We planned this for weeks!" she said.

Mom smiled. "Every good trip needs a Plan B."

Instead, the family drove to an old stone fortress on top of a hill. Inside, it was dry. They walked through dark halls with a flashlight, and a guide told them about the people who lived there hundreds of years ago. Shira's little brother, Eitan, found a secret staircase and climbed it carefully.

At lunchtime, they ate their sandwiches in the car and listened to the rain on the roof. In the afternoon, the sun came out, and they saw a big rainbow over the green hills.

On the way home, Shira opened her notebook. Under her map she wrote: "Plan B: sometimes better than Plan A."

passages.title: The Mistake in the Notebook
passages.text:
Hila had worked on her science fair project for two months. Her question was simple: does music help plants grow? She grew twelve bean plants on her windowsill. Four of them heard classical music every day, four heard loud rock music, and four grew in silence. Every evening she measured them and wrote the numbers in a notebook.

The results were exciting. According to her graph, the plants that heard classical music grew the tallest. Her teacher, Mr. Adler, said it was one of the best projects in the class.

The night before the fair, Hila checked her notebook one last time. Suddenly her stomach felt tight. In the second week, she had written some of the numbers in the wrong columns. When she corrected them and drew the graph again, the difference between the groups almost disappeared. All the plants had grown more or less the same.

She went to her mother, close to tears. "If I show the real graph, my project is boring. Nobody will notice the mistake. Maybe I should just leave it."

Her mother didn't answer immediately. Then she asked, "What is a science project for? To win a prize, or to find out what is true?"

Hila didn't sleep much that night. In the morning, she printed the new graph and added a short note: "My first results were wrong because of a mistake in my records. After correcting it, I found no clear difference."

At the fair, one of the judges read the note twice. "Do you know how many real scientists find mistakes in their own work?" she asked. "The good ones are the ones who say so."

Hila didn't win first prize. But she got a special certificate for honest research, and Mr. Adler asked her to explain her mistake to the younger students the following week.

passages.title: The New Player
passages.text:
When Daniel's family moved to Israel from France, he didn't know anyone in his new town. His Hebrew was still weak, and at school he often sat alone during the break. The only place he felt at home was on the basketball court. In Paris, he had played on a team for four years.

Ido was the captain of the school's basketball team. One afternoon, he noticed Daniel shooting baskets alone and was amazed. Daniel hardly ever missed.

"You should come to practice," Ido said slowly, using his hands to explain.

At the first practice, things did not go well. The coach shouted instructions in fast Hebrew, and Daniel didn't understand them. He ran to the wrong places, and some of the players laughed. One boy, Roi, said loudly, "Why do we need a player who can't even understand the coach?"

After practice, Daniel told Ido that he wouldn't come back. Ido thought about it all evening, and the next day he had an idea. He drew all the team's moves on cards, with arrows and simple words in both Hebrew and English. He also taught Daniel the ten words that the coach used most often.

Two weeks later, in the most important game of the season, the score was tied with ten seconds left. The coach called one of the moves from Ido's cards. Daniel knew exactly where to run. He caught the ball and scored.

In the locker room, Roi came over to him. "I was wrong," he said, and he held out his hand. Daniel shook it and smiled. "Thanks," he answered, in Hebrew.

passages.title: How Bees Give Directions
passages.text:
A honeybee colony can have tens of thousands of bees, but it has only one queen. Her job is to lay eggs. Almost all the other bees are female workers. They clean the hive, feed the young bees, build wax cells and, when they are older, fly out to collect food.

The food comes from flowers. Bees drink a sweet liquid called nectar, which they later turn into honey, and they collect pollen, which is rich in protein. As a bee moves from flower to flower, some pollen sticks to its body and falls onto the next flower. This helps plants make fruit and seeds. Many of the fruits and vegetables that people eat depend on this process, which is called pollination.

But how does one bee tell the others where the best flowers are? In the twentieth century, an Austrian scientist named Karl von Frisch spent years watching bees, and he discovered something amazing: bees dance.

When a worker finds good food far from the hive, she returns and performs a "waggle dance" on the honeycomb. She runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she circles back and repeats the movement again and again. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food compared to the sun. The length of the waggle shows the distance: the longer she waggles, the farther away the food is. Other bees follow her closely, learn the message and fly off to find the flowers.

In 1973, von Frisch received the Nobel Prize for his work on animal behaviour. Today, scientists are still studying bees, partly because bees in many parts of the world face serious problems, such as disease and the loss of wild flowers. In my opinion, every school garden should grow flowers for bees. It is a small thing, but these tiny dancers deserve our help.

passages.title: Tuesdays with Mrs. Klein
passages.text:
Mrs. Klein lives alone on the third floor of our building. She is ninety, and until this winter she walked to the market every morning with her shopping cart. Then she fell on the stairs and broke her hip. After two weeks in hospital, she came home, but the doctor told her that she couldn't go up and down the stairs for at least two months.

My sister Efrat, who is sixteen, was the first to say something. "She can't cook, and she can't go shopping. Somebody has to help."

At first, I wasn't excited about the idea. I'm fourteen, I have lots of homework, and I'm not a good cook. But Efrat had already made a plan. She knocked on every door in the building and made a list. Each family would cook dinner for Mrs. Klein one evening a week. Our family got Tuesdays.

On the first Tuesday, Efrat and I made vegetable soup. We followed our grandmother's recipe, but I added too much salt, and we had to start again. When we finally carried the pot upstairs, Mrs. Klein was waiting by the door. She had put on a nice dress, as if guests were coming. Of course, guests were coming. We were the guests.

She asked us to sit down. While she ate, she told us stories about our street sixty years ago, when there were orange groves where the shopping centre is now. I didn't look at my phone once.

Mrs. Klein can walk up and down the stairs again now. She doesn't need our dinners any more, but Efrat and I still go up every Tuesday. Now she cooks for us.

passages.title: The Second Seat
passages.text:
For three years, Yael had dreamed of becoming the first violin, the leader of the youth orchestra. It was the seat right next to the conductor, the one whose player performs the solos, tunes the orchestra and shakes the conductor's hand at the end of each concert. When Rivka, the old leader, finished high school, everyone assumed the place would go to Yael. She practised two hours a day, and she had never missed a rehearsal.

The auditions were held behind a curtain, so the judges could hear the players but not see them. A week later, the list went up on the noticeboard. Yael read it twice before she understood. First violin: Lior Ben-David. Second: Yael Mizrahi.

Lior had joined the orchestra only six months earlier. He was quiet, a year younger than her and, she had to admit, very talented. Yael went home and refused to talk to anyone. That night she seriously considered leaving the orchestra.

What changed her mind was a conversation with her grandfather, who had played the cello in an orchestra for forty years. He listened without interrupting, and then said something she had not expected. "When I was young, I also thought the most important seat was the first one. But an orchestra is not a race. The person in the second seat has a job too: to make the leader sound better. If you do that well, people won't notice you. They'll just notice that the music is beautiful."

At the next rehearsal, Yael watched Lior more carefully. She noticed that he was nervous; his bow shook slightly during the solo, and he kept looking at the conductor as if he were asking for permission. During the break, she went over to him. Instead of congratulating him, which would have felt false, she offered him a practical tip about breathing before a solo. He looked surprised, then grateful.

Over the following months, something unexpected happened. Yael began to enjoy her new role. She learned to follow Lior's bow so closely that the two of them seemed to play as one. The conductor said that the violin section had never sounded so united.

At the spring concert, Lior played the solo without a single mistake. When the audience applauded, he did something no leader had done before: he turned around, took Yael's hand and made her stand up with him. She still hoped to be first violin one day. But that evening, for the first time, she understood what her grandfather had meant.

passages.title: The Forgetting Curve
passages.text:
Have you ever studied hard for a test, done well, and then discovered a week later that you could hardly remember a thing? If so, you are in good company. In the 1880s, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus became one of the first people to study this problem scientifically.

Ebbinghaus faced a difficulty. If he tried to memorise poems or real words, his results would be influenced by what he already knew. So he invented a long list of meaningless syllables, such as "DAX" and "BOK", which had no connection to anything in his memory. Then, using himself as the only subject, he learned lists of these syllables and tested how much he remembered after different periods of time: twenty minutes, an hour, a day, a month.

The results, published in 1885, showed a clear pattern that is now known as the "forgetting curve". Most forgetting happens very quickly, within the first hours and days after learning. After that, forgetting slows down, and what remains tends to stay longer. Ebbinghaus also noticed something encouraging: relearning a list he had partly forgotten took less time than learning it the first time. Even "forgotten" information leaves a trace.

Perhaps his most useful discovery was what researchers now call the spacing effect. Ebbinghaus found that repetitions spread out over several days were more effective than the same number of repetitions crammed into one session. Since then, this finding has been confirmed in hundreds of studies, with learners of all ages and with all kinds of material, from vocabulary to mathematics.

More recent research has added another important idea: the testing effect. Trying to remember information, for example by answering questions without looking at your notes, strengthens memory more than simply reading the material again. In other words, the effort of remembering is not a sign that learning is failing; it is part of how learning happens.

What does this mean for students? First, a single long night of study before an exam is one of the least effective ways to learn, even if it feels productive at the time. Second, short reviews spread over days and weeks work better than long ones done all at once. Third, closing the book and testing yourself is worth more than reading the same page five times. Many language-learning apps are built on exactly these principles.

More than a century later, Ebbinghaus's simple experiments with nonsense syllables still influence the way people study and teach.

passages.title: The Wrong Train
passages.text:
It was Thursday, 6:40 p.m. Avi and his younger sister Noga were supposed to be at their grandparents' house in Haifa by eight. It was the first time their parents had let them travel alone, and Avi, who was fifteen, had promised to keep his phone on and to send a message from every station.

At the station in Tel Aviv, the board showed two trains leaving from the same platform within five minutes. Avi was busy buying snacks, and when a train arrived, Noga said, "That's ours!" They jumped on just before the doors closed.

Twenty minutes later, Avi looked out of the window and frowned. The sea should have been on their left. Instead, there were fields and an industrial area that he had never seen. He checked the screen above the door: the train was heading south, towards Beersheba.

His first reaction was panic. His second was to reach for his phone, which was completely dead. He had spent the afternoon playing games on it and had forgotten to charge it.

Noga, who was eleven, looked as if she was about to cry. Avi realised that if he panicked, she would too. He took a deep breath and tried to think clearly. They needed to do three things: get off at the next station, find the right train back, and tell their parents that they were safe.

At the next stop, they got off and went straight to the information desk. The clerk, a tired-looking woman, explained that the next train back would leave in fifteen minutes. When Avi asked if he could use a phone, she hesitated for a moment, then handed him her own.

His mother answered on the first ring. She had already tried to call him four times. To Avi's surprise, she didn't shout. "You made a mistake," she said, "but you fixed it calmly. That's what matters."

They arrived in Haifa at half past ten, two and a half hours late. Their grandmother had kept dinner warm, and their grandfather wanted to hear every detail. Noga told most of the story, and to Avi's relief, she made him sound like a hero.

Later, lying in bed, Avi made a list in his head of what he would do differently next time: check the screen before getting on, keep his phone charged and, maybe, let his little sister read the departure board. After all, she had not been wrong about the platform, only about the train.

passages.title: The Game That Didn't Work
passages.text:
When Eli's younger brothers got bored during the long summer holiday, he decided to design a board game for them. Eli was sixteen and loved strategy games, so he spent a whole week on it. The game was called Desert Caravan. The players were traders crossing a desert with camels, buying and selling spices and trying to avoid sandstorms. There were 120 cards, four kinds of coins and a rulebook that was eleven pages long.

He was very proud of it. One morning he laid the board out on the kitchen table and called his brothers: Shai, who was nine, and Itamar, who was seven.

The first game lasted twenty minutes. That was not because it had finished, but because Itamar left the table and went to play with his toy cars. Shai stayed longer, mostly to be polite, but he kept asking, "Wait, why can't I buy the pepper now?" Eventually he admitted, "It's kind of boring."

Eli was hurt. He wanted to say that they were simply too young to understand it. Then he remembered something he had read in an interview with a professional game designer: "If players don't enjoy your game, the problem is the game, not the players."

So instead of arguing, he did something harder. He asked questions. What was the most fun part? (Rolling the dice and the sandstorm cards.) What was the most boring part? (Waiting, and counting coins.) What would make it better? Itamar thought for a moment and said, "Camels that can race."

Over the next two weeks, Eli rebuilt the game almost from the beginning. He reduced the rules to a single page and cut the cards from 120 to 40. He replaced the four kinds of coins with one. He added camel races and made the sandstorms more dramatic. After every change, he tested the game with his brothers again and wrote down what happened. Some ideas worked immediately; others failed and had to be removed. He also noticed something interesting: the best ideas often came from Itamar, the youngest, because he had no idea how a game was "supposed" to work.

By the end of the summer, Desert Caravan had become the family's favourite game. Even Eli's father, who usually said he was too tired for games, asked to play.

Eli kept the first version in a box under his bed. Sometimes he takes it out and looks at the eleven-page rulebook. It reminds him that the first version of anything is rarely the best one, and that the people who criticise your work can be your most useful partners.

passages.title: The Shrinking Sea
passages.text:
Every year, thousands of tourists come to the shores of the Dead Sea to do something they cannot do anywhere else: lie on their backs in the water and read a newspaper without sinking. The water is so salty, almost ten times saltier than ordinary sea water, that the human body floats on it easily. The salt also explains the lake's name. Fish and plants cannot survive in it, although scientists have found tiny living things, such as certain bacteria, in its water.

The Dead Sea is famous for another reason too. Its shores are the lowest place on land anywhere on Earth, more than 400 metres below sea level. Unfortunately, they are getting lower every year, because the sea itself is shrinking. Since the 1960s, its surface has dropped by more than 30 metres, and today it continues to fall by about a metre a year.

The main cause is simple: less water is flowing in. For thousands of years, the Jordan River carried fresh water into the Dead Sea from the north. During the twentieth century, as the population of the region grew, the countries in the area began to use more and more of the river's water for drinking and farming. Today only a small part of the original flow reaches the sea. At the same time, the hot, dry climate causes large amounts of water to evaporate. In addition, mineral companies pump water into shallow pools in the south, where it evaporates and leaves behind valuable minerals.

The results can be seen clearly along the shore. Beaches and buildings that were once at the water's edge now stand far from it. Even more worrying are sinkholes: deep holes that suddenly open in the ground. As the sea goes down, fresh underground water dissolves layers of salt below the surface, leaving empty spaces. Eventually, the ground above them collapses. Thousands of sinkholes have appeared around the Dead Sea, damaging roads, farms and buildings, and some areas have been closed to visitors.

Can the Dead Sea be saved? Over the years, experts have suggested several solutions. One idea was to bring water from the Red Sea through a long pipeline. Others believe that the answer is to let more water from the Jordan River flow south again. So far, none of the major plans has been carried out, partly because of their high cost and partly because of concerns about their effect on the environment.

The Dead Sea will not disappear completely. As it gets smaller, its water becomes even saltier and evaporates more slowly. But without action, the lake that visitors know today will continue to change, and the lowest place on Earth will keep getting lower. In my view, protecting it is a responsibility shared by everyone who lives in the region.

passages.title: The Man Who Was Left Out
passages.text:
The assignment sounded straightforward enough: interview an older relative, record their memories, and turn them into a ten-page written account. Most of Adina's classmates chose grandparents who lived nearby. Adina chose her great-uncle Mordechai, who was ninety-five, lived in a retirement home in Jerusalem, and was known in the family as the hero of a story that everyone told at holiday meals.

According to that story, Mordechai had arrived in the country in 1949 as a young man with nothing but a suitcase, and within a year he had built, entirely by himself, the small carpentry workshop that would later support three generations of the family. Adina had heard the story so often that she could have written it without the interview. That, she later realised, was exactly the problem.

She visited him four times, each time with a notebook and a small recorder. At first he repeated the familiar version almost word for word, as if he were reading from a script. But during the third visit, while she was asking about the tools in an old photograph, he fell silent for a long time. Then he said quietly, "I wasn't alone. There was a man named Shimon."

Slowly, the real story emerged. Mordechai had not built the workshop by himself. For the first two years, he had worked alongside an older carpenter who had taught him nearly everything he knew: how to choose wood, how to sharpen a chisel, how to deal with customers who didn't pay. When the older man became ill, the two lost touch, and over the years, as the story was retold, he had simply disappeared from it. "I never lied," Mordechai said. "I just stopped mentioning him. Then everyone forgot, and after a while, so did I. Almost." Then he showed Adina a small wooden box that he kept beside his bed. "Shimon made this for me when I finished my first table," he said.

Adina went home with a dilemma. The assignment required her to write what she had learned, but she suspected that some of her relatives would not be pleased to see the family legend corrected, especially her grandfather, who was very proud of his uncle. On the other hand, leaving Shimon out a second time felt like repeating the original injustice.

She decided to ask Mordechai himself. To her surprise, he did not hesitate. "Write it," he said. "I'm ninety-five. If I don't correct the story now, nobody will. A person who taught you a trade deserves to be remembered."

Adina wrote the account honestly, but carefully. She did not present her great-uncle as a liar, because he was not one. Instead, she described how stories change as they pass from one person to another, and how easily a helper can become invisible. She ended with Mordechai's own words about his teacher.

When her grandfather read it, he was quiet for a long while. Then, at the next family gathering, he asked Adina to read the final page aloud. Since then, the holiday story has been told a little differently. It is longer now and, Mordechai insists, a great deal more accurate.

passages.title: The Disappearing Night
passages.text:
For almost all of human history, the night sky was one of the most familiar sights in the world. Anyone who stepped outside on a clear, moonless night could see thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way stretching across the sky. Our ancestors used the stars to navigate, to keep track of the seasons and to tell stories. Today, for a large part of humanity, that sight has disappeared. A world atlas of night-sky brightness, published in 2016, estimated that more than a third of all people on Earth can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live.

The reason is not that the stars have changed, but that our nights have. Streetlights, illuminated advertisements, office buildings, sports stadiums and car parks send enormous amounts of light into the sky. Much of it is wasted: instead of shining down on the roads and pavements where it is needed, it spreads upwards and sideways, creating a glow over cities that can be seen from many kilometres away. Scientists call this phenomenon light pollution.

At first glance, light pollution may seem like a problem only for astronomers. However, researchers have found that artificial light at night affects many living things. Consider sea turtles. Females lay their eggs on sandy beaches, and when the babies hatch, usually at night, they find their way to the water by moving towards the brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is the sky over the sea. On a beach near a brightly lit road or hotel, the hatchlings may crawl in the wrong direction, away from the sea, and many never reach it.

Birds are affected too. Many species migrate at night, and bright lights, especially on tall buildings, can confuse them, drawing them off course. Some circle lit buildings until they are exhausted; others fly into windows. Insects, which are attracted to lights in huge numbers, are also harmed, and since insects are food for many other animals, the effect can spread through an entire ecosystem.

Humans are not immune either. Our bodies follow a daily rhythm that is controlled partly by light and darkness. In the evening, darkness signals the body to produce melatonin, a hormone that helps us fall asleep. Bright light at night, including the light from screens, can delay this process. For this reason, sleep researchers often recommend dimming the lights and putting phones away in the hour before bed.

The encouraging news is that, unlike many other forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost immediately. It does not stay in the environment: when a light is switched off, the problem disappears with it. Simple measures make a significant difference. Lights can be shielded so that they shine only downwards. Warmer, less blue light can be used outdoors. Lights that are not needed can be turned off late at night, or controlled by sensors that switch them on only when someone passes by.

None of this requires us to live in darkness. It requires us to use light more thoughtfully. Personally, I believe that a clear view of the stars is part of our shared heritage, as worth protecting as an ancient building or a forest. Every child deserves the chance to look up and see the Milky Way at least once.

passages.title: Arguing the Other Side
passages.text:
When the list of debate topics was posted, Michal felt confident. The motion for the regional final was "Schools should replace printed textbooks with tablets", and she had strong opinions on the subject. She loved paper books: their smell, the margins where she could write notes, the way she could remember where on a page she had read something. She was certain that screens were a distraction and that tablets were being pushed into schools mainly by companies that wanted to sell them.

Then the coach announced which side each team would argue. Michal's team would be supporting the motion. She would have to stand in front of an audience and defend tablets.

Her first instinct was to ask for a change, but the rules of the competition did not allow it, and in any case her coach refused to consider it. "Anyone can argue for what they already believe," Mrs. Sharabi said. "The real test is whether you understand the other side well enough to make its best case."

That evening, Michal complained to her grandfather, who had spent many years studying Talmud with a study partner. He laughed, but not unkindly. "In the beit midrash," he said, "we learned that you have not really understood an argument until you can explain it better than the person who disagrees with you. Only then do you have the right to reject it."

Reluctantly, Michal began to research. At first she looked only for weaknesses in the arguments she was supposed to make, almost hoping to prove her coach wrong. But gradually her view became more complicated. She read that digital textbooks can be updated immediately, while printed ones can stay in classrooms for years after their information has become outdated. She discovered that for some students with visual or reading difficulties, the ability to enlarge text or listen to it read aloud made a real difference. She learned that heavy school bags were a genuine concern for many parents and doctors. None of this changed her love of paper books, but she could no longer claim that the other side had nothing worth saying.

The research also made her more honest about her own position. Some of her arguments, she realised, were really just preferences. The smell of paper was a pleasant memory, not evidence.

On the day of the final, Michal spoke clearly and calmly. She did not pretend that tablets were perfect. Instead, she admitted their weaknesses and argued that they could be managed. One of the judges later told her that this was what had made her case so convincing. Her team won by a narrow margin. Michal was pleased, but to her surprise, the victory was not the part of the competition that she remembered most.

Afterwards, a girl from the opposing team came over and asked, half joking, whether Michal had changed her mind. Michal thought about it for a moment. "Not completely," she said. "I still prefer paper. But now I understand why someone might not, and I think that is worth more than winning."
